topTen.name: The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner
topTen.author: James Hogg

topTen.name: Latecomers
topTen.author: Anita Brookner
topTen.comment: The strange, compelling beauty, sadness and wit of Anita Brookner's greatest novel, a story of two men living with traumatic European pasts, has long been underrated.

topTen.name: To the Lighthouse
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: An absorbing masterpiece and one of the greatest works of modernism, at once the story of a family, a marriage, a house, time and mortality.

topTen.name: The Custom of the Country
topTen.author: Edith Wharton
topTen.comment: Savagely brilliant and breathtaking account of American and European society in the early 20th century, and the most lacerating story imaginable of ruthless social climbing and a failed marriage, with an irresistibly awful heroine.

topTen.name: My Ántonia
topTen.author: Willa Cather
topTen.comment: The great and beautiful work of one of the immortal American writers, taking us through memory into the landscape and lives of the midwest, and on a journey into the unforgettable past.

topTen.name: The Beginning of Spring
topTen.author: Penelope Fitzgerald
topTen.comment: The Beginning of Spring is a magical and haunting recreation of Moscow before the revolution, and a compelling story of a bewildered man in love with two people at once. A work of genius.

topTen.name: Family and Friends
topTen.author: Anita Brookner
topTen.comment: A masterpiece, the sad, funny, absorbing story of an immigrant European family in England and the complex, intertwined fates of its children.

topTen.name: Reading Turgenev
topTen.author: William Trevor
topTen.comment: Haunting, melancholy, precise and heartbreaking, this perfect novella takes us into the dark story of a young woman in constricting, provincial Ireland.

topTen.name: The Portrait of a Lady
topTen.author: Henry James
topTen.comment: My desert island book, the story of a young woman, between America and Europe, confronting her fate and coming to terms with tragedy and suffering. The greatest novel ever written about human relationships bound inside social demands.

topTen.name: A Month in the Country
topTen.author: JL Carr
topTen.comment: A small triumph, the short, spare story of a two men, just after the first world war, working in a village church to uncover the past; also a poignantly touching love story. A wonderful example of the value of simplicity.

topTen.name: Nora Webster
topTen.author: Colm Tóibín
topTen.comment: Of all Tóibín's marvellous work, this novel of widowhood, mourning, motherhood, childhood and music, set in provincial Ireland, catches deep at the heart.

name: Jon Day
summary: This is of course an impossible task, but here are 10 novels that invariably bring pleasure no matter how often I read them, and seem to grow with me. On another day, a totally different 10.

name: Amanda Craig
summary: There are a multiplicity of other titles and authors I would loved to have included, from EM Forster to George Eliot, but I thought I'd widen the net a little.

topTen.name: Small Things Like These
topTen.author: Claire Keegan
topTen.comment: A novel of deepest humanity, compassion and excruciating moral choice, inspired by Ireland's Magdalene laundries and its capture by the Catholic church. A man's whole life in 114 pages. Bill Furlong must choose between helping a barefoot teenager escape from the convent where she has recently given birth , or preserving his own family and business as a coal merchant one freezing Christmas Day, thus exposing the horror and cruelty his community refuses to acknowledge. A modern masterpiece, as pointed and deadly as an icicle aimed at the heart, it should have won the Booker.

topTen.name: Anna Karenina
topTen.author: Leo Tolstoy
topTen.comment: Two stories of an unhappy and a happy marriage are intertwined in this sublime novel, though only the unhappy one tends to be remembered. Beautiful Anna is bored by her marriage to the stiff civil servant Karenin, by whom she has one son. When she is swept off her feet by the dashing Count Vronsky, she scandalises Moscow by leaving her husband and child, ultimately committing suicide. But her brother Levin and his wife Kitty grow into a different and wiser union. Tolstoy's insights into the human heart are deeper than any, and often leavened by unexpected humour.

topTen.name: Great Expectations
topTen.author: Charles Dickens
topTen.comment: A masterpiece about a boy's journey into manhood, and Dickens's greatest work. Thrilling, vivid, suspenseful and as mysterious as the fairytales it draws on, Pip begins as a poor orphan whose act of charity on behalf of an escaped convict changes his whole life. He falls hopelessly in love with beautiful but heartless Estella, another damaged orphan manipulated by an older adult, Miss Havisham. Their lives are connected in a profoundly satisfying way, and Dickens's vigorous, sinewy style conjures London in all its faces.

topTen.name: Persuasion
topTen.author: Jane Austen
topTen.comment: Austen's most mature and affecting novel about heartbreak, disappointment, frustration and second chances. Anne Elliot is her most fully realised Cinderella, whose hopes and looks have been almost extinguished after rejecting, on advice, the poor but brilliant Captain Wentworth. Now rich and distinguished, he has returned victorious, but Anne suffers the snobbery and stupidity of her family before finding release into happiness. A novel that never loses its power, Austen's satirical pen draws on emotions of sorrow, self-sacrifice and regret in a way that deepens and amplifies what could be a purely romantic love story.

topTen.name: A Fine Balance
topTen.author: Rohinton Mistry
topTen.comment: India's Dickens, shamefully overlooked by the Booker, produced a modern masterpiece in this panoramic, multi-layered exploration of rich and poor.  This story of how two lower caste men come to live with a middle-class woman and her nephew in the 1970s, it shows how connected people can be in very different circumstances. It makes you laugh, cry, wince and rage, especially once Indira Ghandi's population policies are put into action.

topTen.name: Vanity Fair
topTen.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
topTen.comment: A satirical delight, set in the time of the battle of Waterloo, this features two women and two men in a quadrille of love, calculation, misunderstanding and naivety. Becky Sharpe, Thackeray's upwardly mobile antiheroine has her foil in pretty, sweet but silly Amelia, Like all Victorian women they must marry or sink, but while Becky climbs ever-upwards in society, Amelia sinks once her father loses most of his money. She marries the spoilt and heartless George Osborne instead of his faithful friend Dobbin. Wickedly funny and propulsively entertaining it is the polar opposite to George Eliot's virtuous Middlemarch.

topTen.name: The Great Gatsby
topTen.author: F Scott Fitzgerald
topTen.comment: The Great American novel was written over 100 years ago, and still contains the essence of America in its account of how a mysterious, fabulously wealthy man tries to woo back the married love of his life by throwing lavish parties. A tale of love, madness, greed, selfishness and the way money corrupts all it touches, its perfection has never been matched.

topTen.name: The Left Hand of Darkness
topTen.author: Ursula K Le Guin
topTen.comment: A groundbreaking feminist masterpiece this explores both politics and gender through SF. Its narrator is a Black male ambassador from Earth sent to Gethen, a planet of perpetual winter where people are androgynous until, at the peak of their sexual cycle they can become male or female. Exiled with a disgraced politician, he undertakes an epic quest in attempting to connect the planet to the Ekumen, a kind of interplanetary UN. A work of visionary imagination and originality, it is also about love, loyalty, humanism and suffering.

topTen.name: Suite Française
topTen.author: Irène Némirovsky
topTen.comment: Had she lived to complete all five parts of her novel, I believe that the Russian Jewish author Irène Némirovsky would be spoken of as the female Tolstoy. Her range and perceptiveness into a variety of characters is as great, as she follows her cast of characters fleeing from Paris before the Nazis arrive in June 1940, through the chaos of France to the countryside. It was a journey Némirovsky made herself, though unlike her characters she had to wear the Jewish star and was ultimately deported and murdered in Auschwittz.

topTen.name: Tom Lake
topTen.author: Ann Patchett
topTen.comment: Very few novels address parenthood, but this is one of them, and it is a gem. A cherry farmer's wife tells her three daughters the story of her affair with a fellow actor some 30 years before they were born. The actor became a world famous film star, whom we gradually learn has just died, and one of the narrator's daughters hopes she might be his daughter. However, we learn how a better, wiser, truer love emerged. A riff on Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard, this is about the hard rewards of farming, family and real life.

topTen.name: The Spy Who Came in From the Cold
topTen.author: John le Carré

name: Sarah Moss
summary: As I get older, I've become franker about what I value most in a novel, which is the unusual combination of artistic brilliance and love of the world. I can admire either, but I return to books that manage both.

topTen.name: The Country of the Pointed Firs
topTen.author: Sarah Orne Jewett
topTen.comment: Quiet technical brilliance - beautiful triangulation of first-person narrator, author, characters - acutely sensitive rendition of setting and sensory experience; precise, ambivalent writing about solitude, loneliness, community; just enough structure to hold while resisting easy ideas about plot. Underrated!

topTen.name: Shadows on the Rock
topTen.author: Willa Cather
topTen.comment: Beautifully crafted writing about long ago and far away, sensitive to the politics of colonialism, power and organised religion while revelling in the art of daily life. I like it when writers approach women's work as the basis of art.

topTen.name: I Capture the Castle
topTen.author: Dodie Smith
topTen.comment: It's both technically wonderful and reliable fun to (re-)read - admirable three-part structure, unreliable but funny and lovable first-person narrator; a version of Englishness that's both knowing and affectionate and the first sentence is unbeatable.

topTen.name: Haroun and the Sea of Stories
topTen.author: Salman Rushdie

topTen.name: Wuthering Heights
topTen.author: Emily Brontë
topTen.comment: My first introduction to the tragedy of romance.

topTen.name: The Slap
topTen.author: Christos Tsiolkas
topTen.comment: My favourite novel of the 21st century so far.

topTen.name: The Cider House Rules
topTen.author: John Irving
topTen.comment: Reading it aged 16 convinced me that I wanted to be a writer.

topTen.name: David Copperfield

topTen.comment: The only novel I've read more than three times.

topTen.author: William Somerset Maugham
topTen.comment: One of the greatest of all novelists, underrated today.

topTen.author: Agatha Christie
topTen.comment: The twist.

topTen.name: The Buddha of Suburbia
topTen.author: Hanif Kureishi
topTen.comment: Mischievous, hilarious, heartbreaking, groundbreaking, one of the best opening lines of all time, manages to be light on its feet, fiercely political and surprising in all its left turns.

topTen.name: Nw

topTen.comment: The best novel about a city that's ever been written.

topTen.name: Family Life
topTen.author: Akhil Sharma
topTen.comment: What it manages to achieve in sparing, precise, concise prose is both devastating and enthralling.

topTen.name: Sag Harbor
topTen.author: Colson Whitehead
topTen.comment: Hilarious, breezy coming-of-age story about the awkwardness teenagers trying to find themselves over a summer during the infancy of rap.

topTen.name: Problems
topTen.author: Jade Sharma
topTen.comment: Jade Sharma's story is tragic and she wrote one perfect, brittle, complex book. It deserves a wider audience. This is an uncomfortable, bleak and sometimes hilarious book about bad relationships, bad drugs and fucked up people trying their best.

topTen.name: Exit West
topTen.author: Mohsin Hamid
topTen.comment: If there was a book that spoke to our times now, it's this one.

name: Yael van der Wouden
summary: Each of these novels have, in one way or another, fundamentally changed my relationship to one of three things: history, language, empathy. For me those are the most important lenses through which one can relate to the world.

name: Benjamin Myers
summary: I have chosen 10 titles that I feel have advanced what it is the novel can – and should – do, while also taking into considering the influence each has had on my own reading enjoyment and writing career.

name: John Self
summary: I chose only books that really mean something to me – there are so many great novels that I thought there was no point in choosing by reputation alone, or books that I think really good but that don't feel personal to me.

topTen.name: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
topTen.author: Muriel Spark

topTen.name: Wuthering Heights
topTen.author: Emily Brontë
topTen.comment: The intensity! The drama! The moors! The sheer weirdness of tiny, fierce Emily B inventing it all in a tiny West Yorkshire parsonage. There is no book like it and no imagination like hers.

topTen.name: Our Mutual Friend
topTen.author: Charles Dickens
topTen.comment: Sprawling and majestic, the whole world is here. Dickens at the height of his powers.

topTen.name: Midnight's Children
topTen.author: Salman Rushdie
topTen.comment: A novel that reimagined what a novel could do, showing us how brilliantly fiction contends with history.

topTen.name: Go Tell It on the Mountain
topTen.author: James Baldwin

topTen.name: Persuasion
topTen.author: Jane Austen
topTen.comment: You would want to be sat next to clever and vivacious Lizzy Bennett at a party, but it's quiet and steady Anne Elliot that you would want as friend. Persuasion is every bit as romantic as Pride & Prejudice. But there's no finer novel at capturing heartbreak – and the relief of reconciliation –  than Persuasion.

topTen.name: The Sellout
topTen.author: Paul Beatty
topTen.comment: Scathing, brilliant, fall over funny. Has any else understood/still understands America better?

topTen.name: Right Ho, Jeeves
topTen.author: P. G. Wodehouse
topTen.comment: Any of the Jeeves and Wooster stories will make your day, but Wooster persuading hapless Gussie Fink-Nottle to dress as Mephistopheles for a costume party is an absolute tonic. Will he win the heart of Madeline Bassett? Probably not.

topTen.name: Those Who Leave and Those Who Stay
topTen.author: Elena Ferrante

topTen.author: Muriel Spark

topTen.author: Vikram Seth
topTen.comment: A dazzling marvel of poetic technique; whisper it, it outstrips its inspiration, Eugene Onegin, and 40 years on, is still prophetic about modern urban living, and the rise of Silicon Valley.

topTen.name: Anna Karenina
topTen.author: Leo Tolstoy
topTen.comment: Beat by beat – heart beat by heart beat, rather – this remains astonishing in its ability to take you into upending force that love can be.

topTen.name: Middlemarch
topTen.author: George Eliot
topTen.comment: Succinctly: this is what it is to be human.

topTen.name: Vanity Fair
topTen.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
topTen.comment: Becky Sharp as the model for how to thrive in the modern world? Still no better guide to surviving in a rapacious world.

topTen.name: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman
topTen.author: Laurence Sterne
topTen.comment: No Tristram, no whimsicality in modern novels. Discuss.

topTen.name: Wittgenstein's Mistress
topTen.author: David Markson
topTen.comment: Perhaps the truest apocalyptic novel we have, because it shows us that the end of the world will be when we as humans have no one left to use language with; a lesson that gains more force every passing day.

topTen.name: Midnight's Children
topTen.author: Salman Rushdie
topTen.comment: Rich, a boundless riot of linguistic imagination and fireworks.

topTen.name: A Place of Greater Safety
topTen.author: Hilary Mantel
topTen.comment: Beyond the events, the people in a pivotal moment of history come vividly to life. The insight into motivations is acute, and there is much more action here than the more celebrated Cromwell trilogy.

topTen.name: The Radetzky March
topTen.author: Joseph Roth
topTen.comment: The best single account of what happens as an empire – any empire – dissolves. While the particularities of the Austro-Hungarian regime are detailed lovingly, its the sense of decay and nostalgia that really lingers.

topTen.name: Oscar & Lucinda
topTen.author: Peter Carey
topTen.comment: Characters as big, as fallible and as indelible as the canvas they're painted on. The image of the glass church sailing inland up the river lives with me still nearly 30 years after first reading the book.

name: Blake Morrison
summary: I've chosen English-language novels that have stood the test of time for a very long period, which has (alas) meant omitting titles from the past 70-plus years such as Lord of the Flies, Catch-22, The Bell Jar, A Clockwork Orange and JM Coetzee's Disgrace, not to mention numerous winners of the Booker and International Booker prize and some tremendous novels in translation.

topTen.name: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy
topTen.author: Laurence Sterne

topTen.name: Bring up the Bodies
topTen.author: Hilary Mantel
topTen.comment: This represents the whole trilogy

topTen.name: Love in the Time of Cholera
topTen.author: Gabriel García Márquez

topTen.name: The Bridge on the Drina
topTen.author: Ivo Andrić
topTen.comment: The paradigmatic historical novel, which shows how society is an historical palimpsest. This is the novel for which, effectively, Andrić won the Nobel prize. In it, he narrates with passion and compassion the tragic history of that contested region which lies between Vienna and Istanbul, encapsulating it in the story of one small town, Višegrad, on the River Drina in Bosnia Hercegovina. I’ve spent a lot of time working with Balkan literature and visiting the region, and I am inordinately moved by this novel which explains it so well.

topTen.name: Frankenstein
topTen.author: Mary Shelley
topTen.comment: An astonishing achievement for its teenaged author, who created a myth and two enduring archetypes in just 18 months: something it usually takes societies centuries to manage. The writing is as fresh as it was two centuries ago, and the Russian doll structure elegant. Since publishing a biography of Mary Shelley in 2018 I’ve not stopped thinking and talking about the author and her first novel – yet it seems inexhaustible, endlessly offering up new resonances and meanings from the failures of the French Revolution to the risks of AI.

topTen.name: The Alexandria Quartet
topTen.author: Lawrence Durrell
topTen.comment: This postcolonial masterpiece tells and retells its story, so that we gradually understand it’s not a conventional novel in which the white western male gets or doesn’t get the girl. Instead, this protagonist is surrounded (and played) by the Egypt’s dawning nationalist movement with its much higher stakes: and doesn’t even realise. This astonishing evocation of cosmopolitan Alexandria summoned me from my small-town life, making me believe in the life to be found in cities, in the wide world - and (by way of Cavafy) in poetry.

topTen.name: To the Lighthouse
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: I would choose anything by Virginia Woolf, in whose hands stream of consciousness is not a trick but an intimate aha!: “Yes, I think like this. So – I’m not odd?” I especially love the “time passes” central section of this novel.

topTen.name: Tamarisk Row
topTen.author: Gerald Murnane
topTen.comment: Gerald Murnane is surely contemporary Australia’s ‘Nobelisable’ novelist (although I also adore Helen Garner, I prefer her nonfiction). His fiction gives us an Australia of the mind by unpicking what “of the mind” really is. Obsessional and hypnotic, it’s writing like no one else’s: and Tamarisk Row is the easiest way in to this strange and yet profoundly common-sensical psychic world.

topTen.name: Pig Earth
topTen.author: John Berger
topTen.comment: This novel built of linked stories creates a portrait of a farming community in the French Alps. But since it's written by Berger, and since that community is isolated and impoverished, Pig Earth also portray the traditions, beliefs and emotions of these people who live almost out of time. And who are everyman and -woman. Berger is always searching out the human meaning, the impulse behind the impulse, and there's nothing sweet about this book. It evokes risk and violence; endurance and dignity.

topTen.name: By Grand Central Station I Sat Down and Wept
topTen.author: Elizabeth Smart
topTen.comment: This short novel and its equally short companion, The Assumption of the Rogues and Rascals, give us mid-twentieth century Britain and America in all its austerity and psychic grimness; yet the books manage to be both explosive and rhapsodic in the telling. This kind of gorgeous, very gendered writing is unusual in the Anglosphere, though there are also Janet Frame and later Beverley Farmer, from NZ and Australia respectively: Smart herself was Canadian. Perhaps the (global) periphery is a good place to write from after all...

topTen.name: We Have Always Lived in the Castle

topTen.name: The Outsider

topTen.name: Wuthering Heights
topTen.author: Emily Brontë
topTen.comment: A forensic look at the destructive nature of passion, and a love letter to the Yorkshire moors.

topTen.name: To Be Taught, If Fortunate
topTen.author: Becky Chambers
topTen.comment: It's a warm, insightful, human view of life away from our planet. It's a response to Joanna Russ's We Who Are About to ... in that it gives hope, rather than despair, in human nature.

topTen.name: Gormenghast
topTen.author: Mervyn Peake
topTen.comment: It's a unique piece of writing; a fantasy with no magic or fantasy creatures; a dark glimpse into the human subconscious and a metaphor for depression expressed in superlative prose.

topTen.name: The Famished Road
topTen.author: Ben Okri
topTen.comment: A unique piece of African magical realism, written in crsip, elegant prose.

topTen.name: Kafka on the Shore
topTen.author: Haruki Murakami
topTen.comment: A playful exploration of coming of age, dreams, reading and the subconscious.

topTen.name: Small Island
topTen.author: Andrea Levy
topTen.comment: A series of interconnected narratives of postwar Britain seen through the lens of race. Magnificent.

topTen.author: James Joyce

name: Beejay Silcox
summary: I decided that the only way to complete this impossible task was to make an argument. Here is mine: the novel is the place we speculate, where we push ideas beyond their limits. These 10 books turn imagination into inquiry, and inquiry back into imagination: a literary ouroboros. They are tales of power and memory, technology and faith, survival and creativity. They ask what it means to have a body and a soul, and what care we owe other bodies and souls. They expand our moral vocabulary, shake our certainties, and make the present – and future – feel contingent rather than inevitable. They are dreams and nightmares, prophecies and farces. And proof that how we dare to imagine the world shapes how we live in it.

name: PD Smith
summary: I've tried to include genre novels and novels written in a foreign language as they are under-represented in such lists of great English fiction. Both are hugely influential in shaping our literary consciousness.

topTen.name: The Man Without Qualities
topTen.author: Robert Musil
topTen.comment: It perfectly captures the period before the first world war in central Europe and anticipates the intellectual uncertainty of the modern era.

topTen.name: Berlin Alexanderplatz
topTen.author: Alfred Döblin
topTen.comment: It is a classic of modernism that captures the essence of one of Europe's greatest cities before it was engulfed by Nazism.

topTen.name: The Trial
topTen.author: Franz Kafka
topTen.comment: Kafka's voice is essential to understanding literature in the 20th century: a pervasive sense of guilt and self-doubt set in an urban context

topTen.name: Bleak House
topTen.author: Charles Dickens
topTen.comment: An unforgettable portrait of 19th-century London, and the wonderful Inspector Bucket is the first professional police detective to appear in fiction

topTen.name: The Maltese Falcon
topTen.author: Dashiell Hammett
topTen.comment: Sam Spade is the classic hardboiled sleuth and this novel transformed the detective genre

topTen.name: The Big Sleep
topTen.author: Raymond Chandler
topTen.comment: Philip Marlowe – the Los Angeles knight – has shaped the detective genre and influenced countless other writers and film-makers.

topTen.name: American Tabloid
topTen.author: James Ellroy
topTen.comment: Ellroy's voice and his detective fiction has captured the violence and misogyny of postwar American culture like no other author. This is his most powerful work.

topTen.name: Titus Groan
topTen.author: Mervyn Peake
topTen.comment: This is the first book in his trilogy. As a work of imagination and fantasy it is unequalled.

topTen.name: Smiley's People
topTen.author: John le Carré
topTen.comment: Le Carré's spy novels, and especially his character of George Smiley, captures something profound about the state of Britain in the Cold War – a country struggling to come to terms with its own decreasing importance on the world stage.

topTen.name: The Valley of Fear
topTen.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
topTen.comment: Although one of Doyle's less well-known detective novels, I think it is fascinating for the way it shows Holmes confronting the reality of the modern world with its themes of lawless American industrial towns and undercover detectives. TS Eliot could recite whole sections of it!

topTen.name: War and Peace
topTen.author: Leo Tolstoy
topTen.comment: The title says it all, or says that the novel is going to try to say it all. But the miracle of Tolstoy’s book is how it can be so monumental while also seething with life and unpredictability. Terror and destruction pervade the book’s panorama of Russian history, and its vision of emotional turbulence. But I find that it remains a weirdly, even exhilaratingly comforting read, because it gives us an entire world to escape into. And that’s why I reread it often, each time finding a new minor character who leaps into unexpected life, but each time also meeting the protagonists as old, complex friends.

topTen.name: Anna Karenina
topTen.author: Leo Tolstoy
topTen.comment: Anna Karenina is famous as an ill-fated love story, but for me the point of the love story is what it releases in Anna herself and therefore the rest of the book. Vronsky isn’t up to her, but that’s not a failing of the book’s, it’s what makes her transformative deepening as a character so resonant, moving and troubling. Rereading it in the past decade, I’ve found it most profoundly a novel about parenthood. The great, tender love scene between Anna and her son Seroyzha more and more seems the book’s centrepiece. It’s a very plotted novel, with an inexorable movement towards Anna’s death, but by weaving between her story and the very different love of Levin and Kitty, Tolstoy gives the book a magnanimous amplitude.

topTen.name: Middlemarch
topTen.author: George Eliot
topTen.comment: The novel at its greatest is for me about holism – about seeing the world, people, events, everything else in all their interconnections and variousness. Middlemarch is the great English novel of holism, because in it Eliot captures all the energy of the nineteenth century within a fastidiously observed locale, whose characters teem with foolishness, goodness, passion, destructiveness, petty ambition, large ideals and much else besides. Eliot learnt from the romantics how to animate character through extremity of feeling. But she writes with such sharpness and patience, and throws her characters into such mundane dilemmas, that the book radiates a steadying wisdom.

topTen.name: Bleak House
topTen.author: Charles Dickens
topTen.comment: Are novels entertainments or deep ambitious works of art? Dickens’s career encapsulates this question and Bleak House encapsulates his career, and it’s the novel where he most abundantly has it both ways. The lunatic comic inventiveness that he extrapolates from the dysfunctional legal system of 19th-century England becomes the very engine of the book’s visionary moral and social intensity. Lady Deadlock is one of the most masterful creations of her century because her character and her personal history are packed with so many of that century’s best and worst possibilities. She’s the haughtiest of aristocrats who’s also a sentimental lost soul who dies scouring the streets for her own past, in the company of a vagabond.

topTen.name: The Portrait of a Lady
topTen.author: Henry James
topTen.comment: So many of the great 19th-century novels come from male writers captivated by trying to write female consciousness. James took this to a new extreme, going so far in one passage as to turn Isabel Archer’s mind into a lavishly envisaged garden that he could walk around inside. Isabel’s desire to live adventurously pushes the plot forwards, and we deeply want to know what’s going to happen to her. But the real action of the book is in James’s luxuriously patient, fervently psychological submission to his own desire to understand her. Of course, she defeats him, but that is his triumph.

topTen.name: Jane Eyre
topTen.author: Charlotte Brontë
topTen.comment: I grew up with Jane Eyre. It was the book that took me from childhood into adolescence; the book where, like so many dreamy teenagers, I found myself reflected as an awkward, reading girl, out of place in my family and social world. I discovered eroticism through fantasising about Mr Rochester; I became a writer through emulating the anger and the wisdom of Brontë’s voice. Jane’s passionate desire for Rochester discovers its own nature through her desperate and regal fury at his destructive self-absorption; she becomes wise through asserting the validity of her own impassioned mind. I haven’t read Jane Eyre for over 20 years. I can’t quite bring myself to reread it, because I can’t bear to find that I love its combinations of gothic extremism and canny realism less than I did.

topTen.comment: The richest late Dickens, full of stuff and connections (I've read it six times and each time I go through it again I notice something new I didn't notice before): both a portrait of the Victorian world and a complex tapestry of theme and symbol. I was sorely tempted to list 10 Dickens novels for this exercise, but have restrained myself.

topTen.name: The Heart of Midlothian
topTen.author: Walter Scott
topTen.comment: People don't seem to read Scott any more, which is a shame: there's a reason why he was the first global superstar of the novel, why the Victorians thought him the greatest writer of his epoch, and this is his greatest work.

topTen.name: The War of the Worlds
topTen.author: H. G. Wells
topTen.comment: The first, and the greatest, alien invasion narrative. It distils global chaos into 200 pages by focusing on the south of England, anticipating modern warfare by projecting it imaginatively onto a Martian incursion: the first novel to represent refugees displaced by war. And the twist ending remains a brilliant coup de theatre.

topTen.name: Beloved
topTen.author: Toni Morrison
topTen.comment: A tour de force, superb style matching powerful subject: an indispensible novel.

topTen.name: The Inverted World

topTen.comment: One of the greatest extrapolations of a core ideas in the rich panolpy of science fiction. Priest at his best.

name: Jeet Thayil
summary: I have left out some obvious titles by American and British and Russian writers. I have little doubt that your other contributors will focus on them, perhaps exclusively. Ten is a tight list. If I had 20, I would have included the obvious and the inevitable.

topTen.name: Rig Veda
topTen.author: Anonymous
topTen.comment: Among the world's oldest books. Combines life advice with philosophy, and reminds us that neither God nor Man can know how the universe was created.

topTen.name: The Divine Comedy
topTen.author: Dante Alighieri
topTen.comment: Terza Rima in the hands of a master, inventor of the most fiendish and intricate of all poetic forms, the canzone.

topTen.name: Ulysses

topTen.name: Pale Fire
topTen.author: Vladimir Nabokov
topTen.comment: Poetry and fiction in inspired collaboration. Nabokov's most playful and erudite work. Reminding us to this day why the novel is called the novel.

topTen.name: Midnight's Children
topTen.author: Salman Rushdie
topTen.comment: This was the novel that opened up the world of Indian writing in English, for better and worse. If not for political considerations, its author would have won the Nobel.

topTen.name: White Teeth
topTen.author: Zadie Smith
topTen.comment: The author was 24 when this debut appeared. It sits firmly in a tradition of the sweeping digressive multi-generational saga. It is also a portrait of Britain and its immigrants, as relevant a portrait as ever.

topTen.name: All About H. Hatterr
topTen.author: G. V. Desani
topTen.comment: This was the novel that made Midnight's Children linguistically, geographically, imaginatively possible.

topTen.name: Silent Spring
topTen.author: Rachel Carson
topTen.comment: Sixty-four years later this book still sounds like modern-day prophecy. Pesticides are in use in many parts of the world. It is also a lesson in how to write the book-length essay.

topTen.name: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland

topTen.comment: Simply a delight.

topTen.name: Middlemarch

topTen.comment: All life is here – slightly marred by its over-earnest protagonist, although there are funny bits too.

topTen.name: Howards End
topTen.author: EM Forster
topTen.comment: Human connection and disconnection: humanism in novel form.

topTen.name: The Gormenghast Novels
topTen.author: Mervyn Peake
topTen.comment: I loved this as a teenager and love it still, for its lush language, its wit, and the vivid mental pictures it leaves with you for a lifetime.

topTen.name: Wuthering Heights
topTen.author: Emily Brontë
topTen.comment: I have read this novel every decade of my life, and it changes its shape every time. A book about obsession, landscape, race, rage, domestic violence, hypocrisy, it transformed what it was possible for women to write. A masterpiece.

topTen.name: Sleeping Murder
topTen.author: Agatha Christie
topTen.comment: The last published Marple novel (though not the last written), it is a dazzling and brilliant recovered memory story, about coercive control, about how sin has a long shadow and how women's reputations are easily destroyed.  A novel far ahead of its time and one of Christie's masterpieces.

topTen.name: The Bluest Eye
topTen.author: Toni Morrison
topTen.comment: Morrison's staggering and brilliant debut novel, published in 1970 and set in impoverished rural Ohio in the 1940s, it is  a razor-sharp laying bare of how racism works and how hierarchies work. Abused and ill-used Pecola compares her life with those of children around her and draws the conclusion that if only she had blue eyes, then everything would be happier and safer.  Reading this in Sussex in the 1970s, it opened my eyes to an entirely different kind of history and catalogue of injustice. It has never dated and still packs a punch.

topTen.name: Demon Copperhead
topTen.author: Barbara Kingsolver
topTen.comment: The winner of the 2023 Women's Prize for Fiction, and co-winner of the 2023 Pulitzer Prize, this is a masterful retelling of Dicken's 1850 classic 'David Copperfield'.  For a modern novel to successfully pay tribute to an older work of genius, mirroring the structure at the same time as making it relevant to the modern day, is rare.  Kingsolver creates brilliant characters and transports issues of poverty and disadvantage to rural America in the grips of an opioid crisis.  Quite simply, a masterpiece.

topTen.name: The Turn of the Screw
topTen.author: Henry James
topTen.comment: The original unreliable narrator, this is a classic of the ghost story genre - creepy children, a governess who may or may not be deluded, or lying, or ill, an isolated country house where nothing is quite what it seems.  It remains as unsettling a read today as when it was first serialised in 1898.  I dare you to give it a go!

topTen.name: The Tale of Genji
topTen.author: Murasaki Shikibu
topTen.comment: This has good claim to be considered the world's first novel, a  written in the early 11th poet, noblewoman and lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu at the Imperial Court.  It is a  fabulously sprawling, soap-opera story about the son of a an emperor and a concubine (Genji), boasting a huge cast, many intertwined storylines.  Radical in its day, not least because it was written in vernacular Japanese rather than Chinese, it gives an amazing insight into a culture and tradition of storytelling long gone.

topTen.name: The Street
topTen.author: Ann Petry
topTen.comment: First published under a male pseudonym in 1946, this was the first novel by a Black woman to sell more than a million copies. Set in Harlem in the late 1940s, it's the story of a determined, resilient, courageous young Black woman, Lutie Johnson, as she tries to raise her son in the poverty, discrimination and violence of the streets of upper Manhattan, where the brave new world promised after the second world war does not exist.

topTen.name: The Pilgrim's Progress
topTen.author: John Bunyan
topTen.comment: Admittedly not the easiest book to read – more than 100,000 words and a continuous narrative with no chapter divisions – it is nonetheless worth the effort. A Protestant allegory, first published in 1678, the book is a dream sequence narrated by the omniscient narrator, Christian, as he journeys to the celestial city burdened down by the knowledge of his own sin. About redemption and transformation, my father read it aloud to me when I was a child, and it had a profound influence on my subsequent writing about faith. A transcendental experience (in a good way!).

topTen.name: Frankenstein
topTen.author: Mary Shelley
topTen.comment: Published anonymously on New Year's Day 1818, this Gothic masterpiece was written when Shelley was only 18 years old and had already suffered a great deal of trauma in her life.  One of the first science fiction novels, it's a story of love and the withholding of love, rather than a critique of man attempting to play God, but it puts the ethics of science firmly in the spotlight and lays bare 19th century terror about disease.  Shelley's extraordinary powers of description - of place, landscape and emotion - are dazzling on every page. Beautiful.

name: Katherine Rundell
summary: Compiling a list of ten felt like committing a minor crime - not to have Go Tell it On The Mountain and Madame Bovary,  Anna Karenina and Wuthering Heights, Gulliver's Travels and Treasure Island, Mrs Dalloway and Jane Eyre, Moby Dick and A Room With a View, Northern Lights and Lord of the Rings, The Lady With the Dog and L'Etranger, The Wizard of Earthsea and Pippi Longstocking, Barchester Towers and Pale Fire, Three Men in a Boat and The Inimitable Jeeves: books that have given me some of the richest pleasure of my life. I'm still unsure about Ulysses, because - titanically great though it is, should a book be in your top ten if it took you ten attempts to finish it? But the ten here are the books that thrill me to think of them - books that see our failure and dread, loneliness and humiliation, and simultaneously salute human endurance, invention, comedy, skill, difference, wit, care, infinite variety and tenacity of love. I consider it an honour to follow those writers anywhere they take us.

name: Natasha Walter
summary: Of course the ranking is almost random; it's impossible to set these books against one another. There were others bubbling under all the time, but in the end these ones kept rising up. When I went back to them as I was writing up this list, I was always surprised by how much more alive and vivid they were than I remembered. Rereading is always the test. But I feel strongly aware that there are so many books, so many writers, that could be on this list – including so many that I haven't yet read.

topTen.name: The Years
topTen.author: Annie Ernaux
topTen.comment: Close up and wide screen, the intersection between the personal and collective has never been so vividly explored. Every sentence is an arrow.

topTen.name: Beloved
topTen.author: Toni Morrison
topTen.comment: Nobody expresses the dehumanisation of slavery with as much humanity as Morrison, nobody communicates the loss of dreams with such imagination.

topTen.name: War and Peace
topTen.author: Leo Tolstoy
topTen.comment: Baggy, undisciplined, exhausting, it's at least three books in one. I hate many of the characters - even the apparently lovable ones - but even at this distance they are still completely alive.

topTen.name: All Our Yesterdays
topTen.author: Natalia Ginzburg
topTen.comment: Ginzburg is an absolute genius at showing the impact of politics and war on intimate lives. A book that is impossible to summarise, its voice is so distinctive and so spiky.

topTen.name: Things Fall Apart
topTen.author: Chinua Achebe
topTen.comment: It still shocks. Empire is still the wound that hasn't healed.

topTen.name: To the Lighthouse
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: How can women be creative in a patriarchal world? This is such a perfect exploration of that conundrum. The composition is exquisite and, bits of it are quite funny - few people give Woolf credit for that humour.

topTen.name: My Brilliant Friend
topTen.author: Elena Ferrante
topTen.comment: I wasn't sure whether to choose this or the second one of the quartet, which I prefer, but I felt that it would be strange to skip over the beginning. Ferrante's world is so complete and so compelling from start to finish.

topTen.name: Nervous Conditions
topTen.author: Tsitsi Dangarembga
topTen.comment: How can you find a path forward when patriarchy and empire keep distorting everything around you? That makes this book sound didactic - and yes, it teaches you a lot - but it doesn't stop Tambudzai's struggle being moving and vividly alive.

topTen.name: The Golden Notebook
topTen.author: Doris Lessing
topTen.comment: Lessing's honesty about women's lives is endlessly discomforting and invigorating. I keep thinking this novel will have dated terribly, but whenever I go back to it I'm compelled again.

topTen.name: Sons and Lovers
topTen.author: D. H. Lawrence
topTen.comment: Lawrence is so out of fashion now, but this novel never loses its force. It journeys from the Victorian to the modernist sensibility, from the working class childhood to the searching adult artist. Despite all Lawrence's limitations, his vision and his world are completely alive.

topTen.name: Ulysses
topTen.author: James Joyce
topTen.comment: The novel that both buries the 19th-century realist novel and opens up superbly rich possibilities for all the novels that come after.

topTen.name: Lolita
topTen.author: Vladimir Nabokov
topTen.comment: Nabokov's masterpiece, which means the best novel by one of the most gifted prose stylists in English. A novel built of the blackest ironies and of the most subtle morality.

topTen.name: Mrs Dalloway
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: Woolf's most humane and beautiful book, brilliantly patterned, a technical marvel.

topTen.name: Money
topTen.author: Martin Amis
topTen.comment: The key postwar English novel: a postmodern black comedy that gives us one of the most fully realised and memorable narrators in the history of the novel.

topTen.name: The Sound and the Fury
topTen.author: William Faulkner
topTen.comment: A novel about the American tragedy - slavery and its aftermaths - as told through the decay and collapse of one Southern family in the early 20th century. A virtuoso work of modernism, and Faulkner's best book.

topTen.name: Heart of Darkness
topTen.author: Joseph Conrad
topTen.comment: Published in 1899, Heart of Darkness condemns 19th-century Europe and prefigures the 20th-century world – it is both about imperialism and, proleptically, about the Holocaust, Stalinism, Mao's China, Vietnam, Pol Pot's Cambodia... A book that we cannot live without.

topTen.name: Madame Bovary
topTen.author: Gustave Flaubert
topTen.comment: With the publication of Madam Bovary, the novel came of age as an artform. All novelist since have worked in the shadow of Flaubert, and of Flaubert's precise, poetic realism.

topTen.name: The Corrections
topTen.author: Jonathan Franzen
topTen.comment: The last Great American Novel, appropriately published on the eve of the September 11th attacks. A novel about a dyfunctional family, the Lamberts, that is also a novel about a dysfunctional America in the age of Neoliberalism - and a brilliantly written one.

topTen.name: Herzog
topTen.author: Saul Bellow
topTen.comment: The best postwar American novel. Despite its misogyny! Bellow wrote an incomparably rich prose, and in Herzog that prose is at its richest.

topTen.name: The Portrait of a Lady
topTen.author: Henry James
topTen.comment: James is perhaps the greatest novelist who ever lived. This novel is the book in which he invented a new way of writing about consciousness and behaviour; all succeeding novelists are in his debt.

topTen.author: Jane Austen

topTen.name: Kindred
topTen.author: Octavia E Butler
topTen.comment: Addressing the still-raw subject of slavery in America through a moving and original take on the time-slip fantasy, a book to read and re-read.

topTen.name: Jane Eyre
topTen.author: Charlotte Brontë

topTen.comment: The great American novel, imo

topTen.comment: The world's first novel has to be on this list. Coming from such a different culture, it is both alien and fascinating, to a modern Anglophone reader, as gripping as a great fantasy novel with a swoon-worthy hero.

topTen.name: The Golden Notebook
topTen.author: Doris Lessing
topTen.comment: Lessing isn't talked about so much recently, but she was and still is a hugely important writer whose best work should still be read.
