name: Catherine Taylor
summary: I wish I had 10 more to choose because I left out some of my favourite writers – Dickens, Austen, George Eliot, Philip Roth, James Baldwin,Toni Morrison, as well as the great French and Russian classics, and indeed novels from my home country of New Zealand such as The Bone People or Owls Do Cry. But I wanted to get a wide scope of the books which have shaped my thinking, some of the most influential and brilliantly written that I've read and, crucially, go back to read. That I feel is an important distinction in these choices.

topTen.name: The Makioka Sisters
topTen.author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki
topTen.comment: An immensely readable and intimate saga (published in English in 1957 in a translation by Edward G Seidensticker) of a vanishing way of life as four sisters in Osaka navigate the years 1936 to 1941 in a changing Japan, and the disintegration of their upper middle class, suburban lives. It contains one of the most startling closing lines in all literature: “Yukiko's diarrhea persisted through the 26th, and was a problem on the train to Tokyo.”

topTen.name: The Golden Bowl
topTen.author: Henry James
topTen.comment: James is often criticised for writing some of the longest paragraphs in the English language, but this novel of two impoverished lovers who marry, respectively, a wealthy father and his daughter – with every intention of continuing their affair – is violently modern, erotic, tragic, all the more so considering it was first published in 1904.

topTen.name: All Our Yesterdays
topTen.author: Natalia Ginzburg
topTen.comment: Ginzburg's epic novel about family, friends and partisans under fascism in Italy and then German occupation from 1943 is a wonder of prose, beautifully translated by Angus Davidson in the 1952 edition. War is a backdrop to domestic concerns as 16-year-old Anna navigates her way through life, but it comes to the forefront when she gets pregnant by a young irresponsible man and then marries an older one, who turns out to be one of the great unsung heroes of a community in peril. Shocking, funny, unsentimental.

topTen.name: Villette
topTen.author: Charlotte Brontë
topTen.comment: One of the weirdest books I've ever read - Brontë's claustrophobic, highly melodramatic third novel (1853) , the last to be published in her life time and written soon after the deaths of her sisters and brother. It boasts an unreliable narrator par excellence in friendless orphan Lucy Snowe, mysteriously exiled to Villette to work in a girls school (based on Brussels, where Brontë worked as a governess in the early 1840s) ) following an unspecified family catastrophe. Brontë anticipates Henry James  in a powerful and ghostly story of independence, loneliness and  isolation.

topTen.name: Blood Meridian
topTen.author: Cormac McCarthy
topTen.comment: McCarthy is one of the greatest prose stylists of all time, and this novel is sheer dance of linguistic virtuosity.

topTen.name: Hunger
topTen.author: Knut Hamsun
topTen.comment: An extraordinary novel about the inward life of a writer whose observations about himself and the shrinking world he lives in is simply powerful.

topTen.name: Arrow of God
topTen.author: Chinua Achebe
topTen.comment: A landmark novel about the falling of a civilization under peculiar strains.

topTen.name: Cry, the Beloved Country
topTen.author: Alan Paton
topTen.comment: A powerful novel about justice and injustice and race, told with a melodic and unusual third person narrator.

topTen.name: The Waves
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: This book breaks the mould of how stories can be told, if or not one can write a novel about a crowd. She does it with sheer brilliance.

topTen.name: War and Peace
topTen.author: Leo Tolstoy
topTen.comment: A mammoth book that defies description as it is about everything and more.

topTen.name: Season of Migration to the North
topTen.author: Tayeb Salih
topTen.comment: One of the most intelligent and undefinable novels - told with gravitas and power.

topTen.name: The Pilgrim's Progress
topTen.author: John Bunyan
topTen.comment: A defining novel in the genre of allegories. It defies age while explaining the tenets of a faith that has shaped the lives of billions.

topTen.name: All Quiet on the Western Front
topTen.author: Erich Maria Remarque
topTen.comment: One of the greatest novels and narrators of any war of all time.

topTen.name: Thirst for Love
topTen.author: Yukio Mishima
topTen.comment: An understated masterpiece about the weight of life as lived in repression.

name: Alex Needham
summary: I clearly like really long books that carefully craft a world and immerse you in it.

topTen.name: Life and Fate
topTen.author: Vasily Grossman
topTen.comment: It's the 20th century War and Peace – writing on the grandest scale, almost cosmic at times, but anatomising the human condition with the utmost scrupulousness and sensitivity.

topTen.name: Pale Fire
topTen.author: Vladimir Nabokov
topTen.comment: The cleverest novelist at his most clever (and funny). Edmind White agreed – and when I interviewed him just before he died he gave me a brilliant mini-tutorial on how this is a gay novel in disguise.

topTen.name: Hurricane Season
topTen.author: Fernanda Melchor
topTen.comment: Reading this feels like being strapped to the undercarriage of a jumbo jet.

topTen.name: The Line of Beauty
topTen.author: Alan Hollinghurst
topTen.comment: A heartbreaking story exquisitely told, it's about the downfall of one person but also of a whole era.

topTen.name: Middlemarch
topTen.author: George Eliot
topTen.comment: The characters and entire mileu are so unnervingly real – how can we feel such an intimate connection with these people living in the provinces circa the corn laws?

topTen.name: Mansfield Park
topTen.author: Jane Austen
topTen.comment: It's her most expansive novel and her most atmospheric. Some people don't like Fanny Price, they're just wrong.

topTen.name: A Rabbit Omnibus
topTen.author: John Updike
topTen.comment: No one's ever captured quotidian life and the humans who live it with such incredible exactness and beauty.

topTen.name: Austerlitz
topTen.author: WG Sebald
topTen.comment: This edges towards a shattering truth in the most oblique and ultimately devastating way.

topTen.name: The Golden Notebook
topTen.author: Doris Lessing
topTen.comment: I felt that reading this not only expanded my mind but sense of empathy for other people – specifically women. It's an incredibly tour of the inside of someone's consciousness and the way that living in the world chafes against it.

topTen.name: Senseless
topTen.author: Paul Golding
topTen.comment: Hardly anyone seems to know about this book and Golding hasn't written anything since, but it's the ultimate in too muchness – decadent, repulsive in places yet also gorgeous.

name: Jennifer Egan
summary: I'm not a huge fan of lists and even less of ranking, though I realise that the internet loves both. Lists have a way of falsely reifying what – for me anyway – are always somewhat instinctive and arbitrary choices. I could as easily have picked 10 different novels, and when I think back on this list, I will likely have trouble remembering which ones I chose. For that reason, I've limited my list to novels written in English; widening the field beyond that felt too overwhelming, and also raises issues of translation, etc, that complicate things unnecessarily.  Also, given that the purpose of this project – which I thoroughly applaud – is to help guide your readers toward novels they might not have encountered, I've tilted my choices toward the past, even the distant past, and suggested some books that I know are less often read in our era of scrolling and choppy concentration.  Quasi-arbitrary though my choices may be, I have zero doubt that they will doubly and triply reward the effort required to read them.

topTen.name: Middlemarch
topTen.author: George Eliot
topTen.comment: It is almost impossible that a perfect novel would also an epic novel – in fact, Middlemarch is the only example I can think of. It's as deeply interior about marriage and sexuality as Eliot‘s era would allow her to be, and yet it's also a sweeping portrayal of England in the grip of tremendous political and technological change, written decades after those changes had happened. There is not a single misstep in this brilliant, engaging and profound study of the rewards and dangers of Victorian marriage.

topTen.name: Pride and Prejudice
topTen.author: Jane Austen
topTen.comment: Pride and Prejudice is a perfect novel, and there are very few. It compresses a complex and perilous social world into an utterly engaging comic satire that exposes the shameful paucity of life choices available to women. Austin‘s method is to keep the darkness at a distance, but it is always present at the edges of her story, adding gravitas. Pride and Prejudice also happened to coin a genre, the romantic comedy, that is thriving to this day. As the kids say, Austen was the OG.

topTen.name: Clarissa, Or, the History of a Young Lady
topTen.author: Samuel Richardson
topTen.comment: A repudiation of Richardson's earlier and utterly ridiculous Pamela, Clarissa is a harrowing indictment of a patriarchy that makes prisoners, victims, and even corpses of its women. Clarissa is shocking and extreme, written in epistolary form in a multitude of voices; an early and inarguable testament to the possibility of writing persuasively across gender.

topTen.name: Invisible Man
topTen.author: Ralph Ellison
topTen.comment: Invisible Man applies the techniques of modernism – its deep linguistic engagement with consciousness – to render the ways in which racism forces people to inhabit incompatible worlds.  Reading this novel feels like gaining a superpower; it made me understand that literature is our best route into modes of perception entirely unlike our own.

topTen.name: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy
topTen.author: Laurence Sterne
topTen.comment: Centuries before Modernism and Post-Modernism, there was Laurence Sterne, who did all of it in one of the first novels ever written in English.  We’ve been trying to catch up ever since!

topTen.name: To the Lighthouse
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: If the modernist project was to map the movement of consciousness using language, I can’t think of a more beautiful – or more economical – novel that accomplishes this. Woolf swims effortlessly in and out of the minds and memories of her indelible characters; moving freely through time and space and somehow managing to create a unified work of art.

topTen.name: The Bluest Eye
topTen.author: Toni Morrison
topTen.comment: The Bluest Eye is an almost forensic expose of the ways in which trauma and oppression lead to madness. I can’t think of a more brutally powerful example of the impacts of American racism on our population. Morrison was one of a kind.

topTen.name: Underworld
topTen.author: Don DeLillo
topTen.comment: I haven't found a more comprehensive and nuanced portrayal of postwar American life than UNDERWORLD, Don DeLillo‘s mid-1990s epic. It synthesizes an era and identifies strands of that American psyche that continue to show themselves in spades: paranoia, creativity, violence. DeLillo is a genius, and this novel is the apotheosis of his powers.

topTen.name: Barchester Towers
topTen.author: Anthony Trollope
topTen.comment: Trollope was the great serialist.  His two major series – each containing six long novels (most of which were published serially) and linking up into an even larger total series, are a big, sprawling masterpiece. It’s hard to single out a single volume when the power of these works is so cumulative, but Barchester Towers, the second book in the first series, is hilarious, moving, relatively compact by Trollope's standards, and contains a number of indelible characters that hold their own in the field of English-language letters.

name: Xan Brooks
summary: The obvious disclaimers. These are my favourite novels, not the best. They are also my favourite novels today. Tomorrow the list would be 50% different. I'm already regretting leaving out Moby-Dick, Slaughterhouse 5 & The Day of the Locust. Damn.

topTen.name: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman
topTen.author: Laurence Sterne

topTen.name: Go Tell It on the Mountain
topTen.author: James Baldwin

topTen.name: Middlemarch
topTen.author: George Eliot
topTen.comment: A novel of the human heart, of politics, of science, of community, of the business and pain of living, about disappointment and endurance and missed opportunities: about life in all its complexity

topTen.name: Ulysses
topTen.author: James Joyce
topTen.comment: Time, history, the mind, a place – expressed in revolutionary form. And with what wit!

topTen.name: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy
topTen.author: Laurence Sterne

topTen.name: Samuel Beckett Trilogy Molloy; Malone Dies; the Unnamable
topTen.author: Samuel Beckett

topTen.name: If on a Winter's Night a Traveller
topTen.author: Italo Calvino

topTen.name: Mrs Dalloway
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: The interior life of a middle-aged London woman turned into high literary art as never before! Some of the most powerful evocations of complicated feelings ever written. Plus the audacious twinning with the tragic Septimus, which makes it a very fine first world war novel too

topTen.name: Emma
topTen.author: Jane Austen
topTen.comment: Of all the books on my list this is the one I think I will probably reread the most times. I love Jane Austen's humour and think her hypochondriacs (including Mr Woodhouse) are some of the funniest characters in all literature. I never know which of my top four Austen novels to single out, but Emma is special because she learns the most about herself, and so earns her happy ending

topTen.name: The Portrait of a Lady
topTen.author: Henry James
topTen.comment: No one writes about excruciating power games better than Henry James. I love the way he spins a web around his characters and the reader even if - as in this novel - you feel desperate for them to find a way out. Of course there isn't one for Isabel Archer, her life is a nightmare and a tragedy, but the way he shows her realising what she has done is so beautiful

topTen.name: Things Fall Apart
topTen.author: Chinua Achebe
topTen.comment: This book made a huge impression on me when I read it and has stayed with me ever since. Encountering such a different world to the one I knew, yet in the familiar form of a short, realistic, character-driven novel, was a remarkable experience. It is a brilliant book that made so many other books possible

topTen.name: The Girls of Slender Means
topTen.author: Muriel Spark
topTen.comment: I chose this for its wittiness about post-war London. Spark's sharp, dry eyes make this crazy household of young women into something extraordinary. The girl who gets stuck in the bathroom window is such a brilliant metaphor. The book was published in 1963 and by then Spark had such a strong vision of what was coming for these young women

topTen.name: Klara and the Sun
topTen.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
topTen.comment: I wasn't sure whether to choose this or The Remains of the Day but chose this because it's about the future and most of my choices are about the past. The way he represents Klara's artificial mind in prose is a stylistic tour de force. But the reason I love this novel so much is because it becomes a fairy tale about a robot who realises what it means to be human

topTen.name: Beloved
topTen.author: Toni Morrison
topTen.comment: Literature tackling history in a new way. So much bravery both in the details of the unbearable story she decided to tell about slavery – and the style that she chose to do it in. One of the best supernatural novels ever written

topTen.name: Jane Eyre
topTen.author: Charlotte Brontë
topTen.comment: The force of Jane's character and one of the most twisted marriage plots

topTen.name: Bleak House
topTen.author: Charles Dickens
topTen.comment: It's a long time since I've read Bleak House but I wanted Dickens on my list because of his incredible narrative drive. This book is one of the great mysteries

topTen.name: My Brilliant Friend
topTen.author: Elena Ferrante
topTen.comment: I haven't reread this since the summer it first appeared in English when I devoured all four novels in the series. I had never encountered a more engrossing fictional account of a female friendship

name: Mark Haddon
summary: I have a terrible memory and when I reread novels they have always changed in our mutual absence (is that not one of the qualities of a really good novel?). I am also increasingly allergic to anything approaching the ideas of a canon. Reading for me is nearly always about looking forward in expectation as opposed to looking backwards in at attempt to catalogue and evaluate. So with two notable exceptions (because I reread both of them every so often) this is simply a list of novels which I have hugely enjoyed read recently.

topTen.name: Jacob's Room
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: Jacob’s Room is the radical novel-without-a-protagonist that should be revered as part of the groundbreaking modernist trio of works that came out in 1922 along with The Wasteland and Ulysses.

topTen.name: Bleak House
topTen.author: Charles Dickens
topTen.comment: The first proper detective novel and a whole grubby, glorious, shadow-filled world in itself.

topTen.name: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter
topTen.author: Carson McCullers

topTen.name: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman
topTen.author: Laurence Sterne

topTen.name: If This Is a Man / the Truce
topTen.author: Primo Levi

name: David Nicholls
summary: More a list of favourites – there are some scandalous omissions that I know others will pick – and definitely skewed towards the books that I read at an impressionable age, but everything here has engaged, affected and influenced me and I love them all.

topTen.name: The Great Gatsby
topTen.author: F Scott Fitzgerald
topTen.comment: A book that seems different every time I read it.

topTen.name: Housekeeping
topTen.author: Marilynne Robinson
topTen.comment: The most exquisite writing - perfect prose on every page. Absolutely heartbreaking too.

topTen.name: Howards End
topTen.author: EM Forster
topTen.comment: By no means a perfect novel but still stuffed full of ideas and with such warmth and curiosity and humour.

topTen.name: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
topTen.author: Muriel Spark

topTen.name: The Transit of Venus
topTen.author: Shirley Hazzard
topTen.comment: All the scale and high emotion of a great 19th century novel, but published in 1980. One of the great endings too - a puzzle that clicks into place and makes you gasp.

name: Marcel Theroux
summary: It bears repeating that choosing the 10 best books is a bonkers exercise on a par with choosing the 10 best people.  It's always going to be an approximate assessment of the books that you find most enchanting, consoling and inspiring. I more and more think that modernism was a con-trick perpetrated on the reading public by a coalition of writers and academics so I couldn't find a place for Joyce or Woolf. The great novels, in my view, don't require special pleading or academic intervention to make you appreciate them. They grab you by your lapels and plunge you into a fictional world that supersedes the one you're in. My list reflects that feeling.

topTen.name: Middlemarch
topTen.author: George Eliot
topTen.comment: Wise, vast, reassuring, anachronistically cinematic.  Great on the page -- and great with Juliet Stevenson doing the audiobook.

topTen.name: Pride and Prejudice
topTen.author: Jane Austen
topTen.comment: Whenever I reread Austen, I'm amazed by her economy and the way her crafty voice anticipates the sleights of hand of modernism.  And it's a great story that whips along.

topTen.name: David Copperfield
topTen.author: Charles Dickens
topTen.comment: Choosing a list of the ten best novels is like choosing a list of the ten best people in the world: ie. subjective and a bit bonkers.  We have Dickens's word that this is his favourite child.  That's good enough for me.

topTen.name: Gulliver's Travels
topTen.author: Jonathan Swift
topTen.comment: An early speculative novel that combines the unselfconscious energy of children's fiction with something dark and strange and scatological.

topTen.name: The Great Gatsby
topTen.author: F Scott Fitzgerald
topTen.comment: I once worshipped this book and I still venerate Fitzgerald's writing.  What's changed for me is my feeling about the story — there now seems to me something slightly sophomoric about it.  And yet, its construction and its characters still shine with an exemplary vividness.

topTen.name: The Master and Margarita
topTen.author: Mikhail Bulgakov
topTen.comment: Channeling, among other influences, H G Wells, and living under in a totalitarian dictaroship, Bulgakov proved that genre is a meaningless construct with this extraordinary religious, historical, satirical, magical realist work that expands your sense of the things that a novel is capable of.

topTen.name: Kim
topTen.author: Rudyard Kipling
topTen.comment: Kipling is a divisive figure, but I believe his genius is undeniable.  The strange lapidary prose of this book is more interesting and readable than the overpraised Moby-Dick or the largely turgid experiments of the so-called modernists.  Edward Said gives a pious summary of Kipling's thought crimes in the introduction to the Penguin edition.  Kipling, who believed he was inspired to write by a daimon, had a visionary power and creative gift that it would be a pity to deprive yourself of because you don't share his views.

topTen.name: The Memory Police
topTen.author: Yoko Ogawa
topTen.comment: It’s a cool, clever dystopian novel where words objects slip away from reality when the words are banned by the authorities. I think it offers a salutary message in a time when words slip from their meanings.

topTen.name: Mussel Feast
topTen.author: Birgit Vanderbeke
topTen.comment: An extraordinary, spare novel about politics and fear, distilled into a terrified family waiting for their father to come home.

topTen.name: A Visit From the Goon Squad
topTen.author: Jennifer Egan
topTen.comment: What a brilliant fractured timeline, unfolding into a complex, glittering narrative. I love this book.

topTen.name: Overstory
topTen.author: Richard Powers
topTen.comment: Someone described it as the Moby-Dick of trees, but it’s better than that.

topTen.name: The Dark Is Rising
topTen.author: Susan Cooper
topTen.comment: This book is a masterpiece and I will not be taking any questions at this time.

topTen.name: The Luminaries
topTen.author: Eleanor Catton
topTen.comment: This was my Booker prize winner, and it deserved to be.

topTen.name: The Green Road
topTen.author: Anne Enright
topTen.comment: Every time I read this book, it gets better. How does she do that?

topTen.name: How to Be Both
topTen.author: Ali Smith
topTen.comment: This book is everything: erudite, playful, thoughtful.

topTen.name: The Noise of Time
topTen.author: Julian Barnes
topTen.comment: I could have picked any Julian Barnes novel because all of them are exquisite. I chose this because it’s opening pages should be studied by everyone who wants to be a better writer.

topTen.name: Tale for the Time Being
topTen.author: Ruth Ozeki
topTen.comment: It is such a joyful book - the story of a miserable teenage girl and the aftermath of a tsunami cannot be so sparky and fun. But it is.

topTen.name: Go Tell It on the Mountain
topTen.author: James Baldwin

topTen.name: Danny the Champion of the World
topTen.author: Roald Dahl

topTen.name: The Waves
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: The ages of man and woman; morning, noon and night; the cycle of the seasons. The pattern of friendship; the wholes we make together as we meet and part. The defiant energy with which we make our own stories while the waves go on breaking. All this is held between the covers.

topTen.name: The Return of the Native
topTen.author: Thomas Hardy
topTen.comment: Figures appear in silhouette against the sky … singly and in groups they’ll come along the path towards us; we’ll know them. But in the mind’s eye we’ll always see them, and see ourselves perhaps, as figures on a wide earth, toiling or triumphing under a great and godless sky. And then the unforgettable scenes Hardy choreographs like no other, so strange yet universal, so tiny and vast: gamblers rolling dice by the light of glow-worms, the red tinge of a reddleman in the night, a mother’s lonely walk.

topTen.name: Jacob's Room
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: With astonishing lightness and economy, dipping here and there into the current of life as it runs on through London streets, across lonely moors, pushing into crowds or standing apart, Jacob's Room conjures one person's presence - and absence. It's about all presence, all absence.

topTen.name: My Ántonia
topTen.author: Willa Cather
topTen.comment: An inexhaustible novel of tough lives and hard-won comforts on the pioneer farms of Nebraska. Every line of it is made to last, and its stilled scenes - both intimate and vast - are emblems to carry in mind. There's plenty of drama but it's in the quiet passages that feeling gathers. For a decade, when I was teaching American fiction, I reread the novel each year before giving a lecture on it. Not once did I manage to skim it, or care a bit less. Its shocks are always new; its steadying power undiminished.

topTen.name: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman
topTen.author: Laurence Sterne
topTen.comment: Sterne’s gloriously looping, dancing routes of digression show us that an efficient narrative line from A to B would miss just about everything that matters. The slightest and the greatest thoughts jostle together while I’ll narrator, assuming nothing, reinvents his book from page to page. Any passage of it is bulwark against bland jargon and faceless AI-speak.

topTen.name: Ulysses
topTen.author: James Joyce
topTen.comment: I nearly left it out, and then missed it from my list: missed the immense fertility by which each phrase generates three or a hundred more, moving through word associations, jokes, jingles, half-lost memories. I missed, most of all, the relationship between ordinary modern lives and Homer’s Odyssey: stories overlaying each other, illuminating each other.

topTen.name: The Good Soldier
topTen.author: Ford Madox Ford
topTen.comment: A man tries to tell his story - not a tragic one, merely sad - as if he were talking with a companion by the fire. His voice runs on through the night, and runs on in the minds of readers. He goes back, he goes forward. The mobility of tone is grippingly strange and yet true - it seems to me - to the experience of life being perfectly ordinary, absurd, agonising and exultant, without any contradiction.

topTen.name: The Mirror and the Light
topTen.author: Hilary Mantel
topTen.comment: Mantel makes time move in extraordinary ways. Because Cromwell fits about a year’s worth of thought and action into every five minutes, time both races by and swells outwards. We know the end, and hold our breath as we travel towards it through a great space of narrative in which the grindingly inexorable mixes with limitless invention and surprise.

topTen.name: How to Be Both
topTen.author: Ali Smith
topTen.comment: Protean, generative, ingenious, leaping with life, Smith grants her readers the super-power of making connections. The linked stories glimmer through each other (like pentimenti visible through painted fresco) and there’s no saying which should take precedence.

topTen.name: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
topTen.author: Muriel Spark

name: Clare Clark
summary: I thought this would be fun and it ended up being the hardest job imaginable. What does the best 10 books even mean? Are they the books that have changed you? That have changed fiction? That you return to the most? What about all the ones you have to leave out? In the end I picked 10 that, if I was cast away with them on a desert island, I would never tire of going back to, that would always give me more.

topTen.name: Madame Bovary
topTen.author: Gustave Flaubert
topTen.comment: Because it set the standard for what novels at their best can do. Flaubert not only shows us the secrets of the human heart, he finds the universal in the personal, the tragic in the banal, the profound truths that are to be found in the petty narrow lives of ordinary people. This novel changed what fiction could do and set the template for every writer who came after.

topTen.name: Middlemarch
topTen.author: George Eliot
topTen.comment: Because of its wisdom, its generosity, its humour, its slyness, its compassion, its deep burning rage. Because every time I come back to it I find more. Because everyone who reads this novel cannot come out of it unchanged, because it makes all of us  better.

topTen.name: Anna Karenina
topTen.author: Leo Tolstoy
topTen.comment: I'm going to stop writing now because my answers feel trite. But suffice to say the people and places in these novels are as real and as important to my sense of self as the real people and places in my life. They have changed me and sustained me and challenged me and broken my heart. I can't imagine life without them.

name: Arifa Akbar
summary: Also wanted to include The Remains of the Day by Kazuo Ishiguro but ran out of options!

name: James Meek
summary: I could easily have chosen 100. By Outline I have in mind the whole Outline trilogy.

topTen.name: A Visit From the Goon Squad
topTen.author: Jennifer Egan

topTen.name: The Story of the Stone, or the Dream of the Red Chamber
topTen.author: Cao Xueqin

topTen.name: A Dance to the Music of Time
topTen.author: Anthony Powell

name: Jo Hamya
summary: I think the relationship one has with their favourite novels is a bit like a romance: life becomes charged, sweeter – more meaningful as a result of spending time with them. There’s an electricity between the prose and the reader that suffuses ordinary time. To a writer, one’s favourite books are also often those you wish you’d written, and which bring out pangs of longing and jealousy as a result. My experiences, and perhaps more importantly, my memories of the experiences of reading these novels have a kind of erotics attached to them. In the way of all good romances, they’ve altered some fundamental part of me.

topTen.name: Lolly Willowes, Or, the Loving Huntsman
topTen.author: Sylvia Townsend Warner

topTen.name: The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny
topTen.author: Kiran Desai

name: Tom Crewe
summary: I suppose if I had a guiding rule here – since of course so many masterpieces have been left off – it was to choose the books that have left the strongest impression in my memory: that when I recall the most revelatory, gripping, pleasurable reading experiences of my life, these are the ones that come first to mind.

topTen.name: The Palliser Novels
topTen.author: Anthony Trollope
topTen.comment: The greatest novel sequence in the English language; but, also, better than Proust. Contains several masterpieces. Unbelievably rich, giving almost all of the pleasures possible in fiction. And one of the great marriages, in Plantagenet Palliser and Lady Glencora.

topTen.name: Anna Karenina
topTen.author: Leo Tolstoy
topTen.comment: What more can anyone say?

topTen.name: The Red and the Black
topTen.author: Stendhal
topTen.comment: The original and best story of the boy from the provinces rising to the top of society, and being corrupted on the way.

topTen.name: Cousin Bette
topTen.author: Honoré de Balzac
topTen.comment: A marvellously, devilishly complex, entertaining, rattling story of a family being destroyed from within.

topTen.name: Middlemarch
topTen.author: George Eliot
topTen.comment: Massive on the landscape.

topTen.name: Mansfield Park
topTen.author: Jane Austen
topTen.comment: Not as dazzling as Pride and Prejudice, or as pleasing as Emma, but with a moral amplitude that takes up more space in the memory.

topTen.name: Les Misérables
topTen.author: Victor Hugo
topTen.comment: Perversely, considering its overwhelming scale and scope, overshadowed by the musical: but still one of the greatest of novels.

topTen.name: Pickwick Papers
topTen.author: Charles Dickens
topTen.comment: Of course Dickens wrote more accomplished novels, but did he ever write anything funnier than his first one? It is one of the most joyful books in English -- like a permanent summer's day.

topTen.name: The Ambassadors
topTen.author: Henry James
topTen.comment: Beautiful in the fineness of its perceptions, its atmosphere, its moral.

name: Charlotte Northedge
summary: In order to tackle this impossible task, I decided to choose books that stayed with me long after reading them and that have meant something important to me at various stages of my life.

topTen.name: Middlemarch
topTen.author: George Eliot
topTen.comment: Both intimate and epic, and one of the most memorable reading experiences of my life.

topTen.name: Persuasion
topTen.author: Jane Austen
topTen.comment: I was tempted to choose Pride & Prejudice, but this is the Austen that moved me more than any other.

topTen.name: To the Lighthouse
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: This and Mrs Dalloway transformed the way I saw writing and the world.

topTen.name: The Great Gatsby
topTen.author: F Scott Fitzgerald
topTen.comment: Slim and stylish with such vivid, memorable descriptions.

topTen.name: Beloved
topTen.author: Toni Morrison
topTen.comment: Powerful, pioneering and devastating.

topTen.name: Never Let Me Go
topTen.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
topTen.comment: There are a number of Ishiguro's books I would have liked to include, but I chose this one for its direct and haunting dystopian vision.

topTen.name: The Handmaid's Tale
topTen.author: Margaret Atwood
topTen.comment: Atwood had to be on my list, and though I wanted to include The Blind Assassin and Cat's Eye, it had to be this classic feminist dystopia.

topTen.name: My Brilliant Friend
topTen.author: Elena Ferrante
topTen.comment: Reading Ferrante's Neapolitan quartet in sequence was an utterly immersive experience and though the second novel was my favourite, you have to start here.

topTen.name: Half of a Yellow Sun
topTen.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
topTen.comment: Epic and memorable storytelling, this novel stayed with me long after I read it.

topTen.name: The God of Small Things
topTen.author: Arundhati Roy
topTen.comment: Haunting and beautifully written, it introduced me to another world.

topTen.name: In the Time of the Butterflies
topTen.author: Julia Alvarez

name: Liese Spencer
summary: There were so many other titles I would have loved to have included but these are certainly a few of my favourites – and I'm happy to put Austen as my number one.

topTen.name: Emma
topTen.author: Jane Austen
topTen.comment: It could have been Pride and Prejudice or Persuasion but I have a soft spot for bossy, meddlesome Emma.

topTen.name: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman
topTen.author: Laurence Sterne
topTen.comment: More than 250 years since it was first published it's still fresh and funny.

topTen.name: Beloved
topTen.author: Toni Morrison
topTen.comment: A gothic horror about slavery that shifts between past and present, real and supernatural - evocative and disturbing.

topTen.name: Mrs Dalloway
topTen.author: Virginia Woolf
topTen.comment: Worlds of ideas and emotion in one slim, supremely readable novel.

topTen.name: Crime and Punishment
topTen.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
topTen.comment: This paranoid, propulsive thriller about guilt, justice and redemption puts you inside the mind of axe murderer Raskolnikov.

topTen.name: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
topTen.author: Muriel Spark
topTen.comment: Elegantly sinister, Spark's beguiling story of a cultish schoolteacher stands the test of time.

topTen.name: Normal People
topTen.author: Sally Rooney
topTen.comment: An intelligent, modern love story driven by Rooney's razor sharp dialogue.

topTen.name: Riddley Walker
topTen.author: Russell Hoban
topTen.comment: Once you tune in to its post-apocalyptic dialect, reading this bleak, futuristic tale is a thrillingly immersive experience.

topTen.name: Housekeeping
topTen.author: Marilynne Robinson
topTen.comment: This luminous story of orphan sisters growing up in remote Idaho is dreamlike and disturbing in its portrait of the precariousness of life.

topTen.author: Muriel Spark

topTen.name: The Trick Is to Keep Breathing
topTen.author: Janice Galloway

topTen.name: Who Will Run the Frog Hospital?
topTen.author: Lorrie Moore

topTen.name: Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead
topTen.author: Olga Tokarczuk

topTen.author: Muriel Spark

topTen.name: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter
topTen.author: Carson McCullers

topTen.name: Bleak House
topTen.author: Charles Dickens
topTen.comment: Charles Dickens' masterpiece.  It has everything.

topTen.name: The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
topTen.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
topTen.comment: Robert Louis Stevenson's satisfying, creepy, succinct exploration of human nature and good and evil.

topTen.name: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
topTen.author: Muriel Spark
topTen.comment: Muriel Spark dusts off Jekyll and Hyde and gives us a charismatic monster reimagined as a prim schoolteacher in Edinburgh.  A real Tardis of a book, much bigger on the inside than the outside.

topTen.name: The Big Sleep
topTen.author: Raymond Chandler
topTen.comment: Chandler brought elegance and a sharp wit to the crime story and helped define the genre, as well as playing merry hell with the American dream.

topTen.name: Crime and Punishment
topTen.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
topTen.comment: The most humane and challenging description of a common murderer whose guilt won't allow him a moment's peace.

topTen.name: A Dance to the Music of Time
topTen.author: Anthony Powell
topTen.comment: A single narrative constructed as twelve episodes.  Brilliantly clever dissection of upper class life in England seen against the backdrop of the whole twentieth century.  Witty and caustic and giving us Widmerpool, one of the most extraordinary characters in all literature.

topTen.name: Song of Solomon
topTen.author: Toni Morrison
topTen.comment: An electrifying novel about Black experience in America, told in the most luminous prose imaginable.  A book I could read again and again and never tire of.

topTen.name: Money
topTen.author: Martin Amis
topTen.comment: An evisceration of greed and delusion and privilege.  John Self is mesmeric, even as he descends into hell.

topTen.name: Lanark
topTen.author: Alasdair Gray
topTen.comment: An extraordinary narrative, unlike anything you will ever read.  It sent jolts through contemporary Scottish writing and helped start many an author's career.

topTen.name: Life After Life
topTen.author: Kate Atkinson
topTen.comment: I marvelled at this book, even as I was reading it for the first time.  Such a vivid imagination, a clarity of purpose, and perfect execution.  It shouldn't work but it does.  Atkinson is a genius.

topTen.name: The Dirty Dust
topTen.author: Máirtín Ó Cadhain
topTen.comment: A gossipy, choral and altogether maddening Irish-language masterpiece. People get scared of the Connemara dialect in the original CRÉ NA CILLE (literally 'Graveyard Clay'), but most of the difficulty actually comes from the structural intricacy of the novel – that is to say, from Ó Cadhain's genius, not from the fact that he wrote in natural native Irish. Of the English translations, the general consensus is that Mac Con Iomaire and Robinson provide a precise academic translation while Alan Titley's takes confident liberties to capture the spirit and the tone.

topTen.name: Arturo's Island
topTen.author: Elsa Morante
topTen.comment: Elsa Morante was not afraid of exclamation marks, nor of writing the sort of gothic page-turner that occasions them. First published in Italian in 1957, L'ISOLA DI ARTURO nonetheless feels almost Victorian in its immersiveness and gleeful doorstoppery excess. There are two main English translations, one by Isabel Quigly in 1959 and another by Ann Goldstein in 2019, with Goldstein's said to more closely reflect Morante's stylistic idiosyncracies.

topTen.name: Song of Solomon
topTen.author: Toni Morrison
topTen.comment: Nobody else can combine Morrison's knowledge of the human heart with her historical rigour and fine-tuned prose. Critics underestimate and reduce her when they call her 'lyrical'; she can pull off any register she wants, and a huge array of them are on display here.
